utterances.text: So you will agree with that. Mr. Tuka, all that winter of 1993/1994 you spent living in fear, wondering when somebody else would appear again with a similar intent.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I think we were all in the same boat, and we were all living in anxiety, in fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you remained detained there long after the Washington Accords were signed, that is, for two whole months after the Accords were concluded. Why was that? Why weren't you released?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I tried to obtain a permit from the military authorities in Fojnica, and four or five times I went to see the deputy mayor of the municipality, and his answer always was, "Well, your case is slightly more difficult. I have to get authorisation from Sarajevo to see what we can do and how," and days went by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, a few words about your views, about your opinion. If I understood you properly, you wanted to be independent.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you wanted to enjoy certain autonomy. I heard that your unit enjoyed certain autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I would not call it independence. We were part of that community except that perhaps our views slightly differed from theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also remember what you said, that you did not obey everybody, that you would you put no blind -- that you would not be blindly anything; you had no blind faith towards anyone. That is what you said in your statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, yes, there is some truth in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for the Vance-Owen Plan, you know that the Vance-Owen Plan said that Fojnica should become part of the Travnik -- rather, the Canton number 10?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, however, and your Muslim colleague, agreed that you should leave the things as they were?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: No. That agreement was reached, that is, in that Travnik region or community. And I don't know what it was to be called. Muslims from Fojnica were to send a representative to be in that community, and they had designated a man, a civilian, who was to do that. And about the other activities, we had received no instructions from anyone; nor I, nor Mr. Beba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, what is the purpose of this cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question about the Vance-Owen Plan, and I believe it will be clear what I was trying to achieve, if I may ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Tell me what the point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no ultimatum addressed by the HVO to the Muslim side. That is what Mr. Tuka was saying a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. You can ask that and we'll be moving on, because you really must be finishing your cross-examination soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, I was about to add to what you just said. There was no ultimatum. You put no ultimatum -- rather, you received no orders to that effect, that you should face the Muslims with an ultimatum or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite the reverse. You say you had established a contact to do something that needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes. They designated a man who was to represent them to be the delegate or whatever in that Travnik community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tuka, some of the documents that you had, you destroyed. You only preserved those documents you thought would be particularly important for you.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, there were things which were really surplus, and I burnt most of it. It wasn't important. One just drags it all around and, I don't know, moving from one place to another, and somebody might use it. To what end, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you also kept a diary for a time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also destroyed that diary?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I hid it at home, and then my sister came, found it and destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that seized documentation, stamps, and everything else of the HVO which the BH army took over after the 2nd of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But don't you think that there is a possibility for the documents to be misused?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, towards the end of 1992 -- I'm trying to draw to a close -- there was a football tournament sometime between the Christmas and the New Year in 1992; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we shall agree that there were both Muslim and Croat teams participating in that tournament, from different towns?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the HDZ leadership from Fojnica, Mrs. Mijatovic, Mr. Mira Tuka, and others asked Mr. Kordic to sponsor the tournament?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't if they asked him, but I do know that the organiser of the tournament, Mr. Fabijan Katanic, was the one who was committed this whole thing. About Mira Mijad, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that at the end of this tournament a small ceremony took place in the hotel in Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were a few people who made some speeches. It was a friendly and solemn atmosphere, and one of the speakers was Mr. Nazir Salimovic, who was the mayor of the municipality of Fojnica, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, he was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among other things, on that occasion he paid tribute to Mr. Kordic for making this effort, for investing this effort into improving the relations between the Croat and the Muslim community, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't really remember what was said on that occasion, but do I know that the atmosphere was friendly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to another subject. Do you know how the demographic structure had changed in Fojnica as against the situation before the war?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Immediately in the wake of the war there were only about 100 Croats in the town itself, and around it, in the area which was controlled by the Muslims of the B and H -- rather, the army of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree that at least 5.500 Croats, perhaps even more Croats from Fojnica, had to leave the territory?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm coming to a close. Mr. Tuka, will you agree with me that in front of you at all those meetings, when you accompanied Mrs. Mijatovic or which you attended alone, that Mr. Kordic never voiced any extremist views?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I could not notice that. There would be discussion, but it was all -- there was always some tolerance, and -- normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we are coming to a close, the document which was produced today, Z1024,1, which is the proclamation of the municipality as a zone of peace. The date of it is the 13th of June, '93, but we agree that was signed on the 30th of June, 1993, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because on that day, General Morillon came to Fojnica, and the signing of this document, the proclamation of the zone of peace, was marked in a ceremony?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I've heard that, but I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we agreed that less than two days later -- and I believe it was Wednesday -- on Friday, the BH army attacked the HVO. We've agreed about that, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment; let me go through these papers. Perhaps I've forgotten to ask a question. Well, perhaps I have concluded. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Tuka. Thank you for your answers. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tuka. My name is Goran Mikulicic. I am from Zagreb, and with my colleague Kovacic I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. I will ask you several questions relative to your testimony here, and I should like to ask you to answer those questions to the best of your recollection. Mr. Tuka, just a few words about the civilian defence, in view of the fact that as a reserve captain, as of 1992, you were responsible for the civilian defence in Fojnica; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Only in the place where I lived, in my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tuka, is it true that the civilian defence was organised under the sponsorship of the Secretariat for National Defence of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the civilian defence had its own chain of command, its own hierarchical structure, which was completely separate from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, the civilian defence was in no way part of the Territorial Defence, was it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I'm somewhat at a loss. I don't know how, exactly, the responsibilities were divided. Perhaps somebody at some point in time would be the commander over both, and I guess it must have happened that at some point, somebody should have both of these under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but I'm referring to the peacetime.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, in peacetime, they were separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we had two separate organisations?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, the civilian defence was organised, it had its so-called platoons, platoons for fortification, for alert, and so on and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But generally speaking, the civilian defence incorporated those persons who were not incorporated in some military activities; that is, men who are not able-bodied, or rather not able for the military service?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, there were some who were able for military service, but by and large, there were women and some elderly persons; all sorts of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the civilian defence units, did they ever organise some drills?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, if you mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In peacetime.

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, in peace, and during that other -- under that other system, yes, that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it true, Mr. Tuka, that the civilian defence also incorporated so-called labour platoons, which simply had some work obligations, such as building the fortifications and things like that?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, is it true that in case of a danger of war, or impending that war, these labour platoons would be used for some war operations; that is, digging in, building fortifications, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, yes, unless they were in the combat zone and threatened with the danger of war. I think that there was a rule to this effect of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tuka, you told us that you joined the political party, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that in that capacity, you attended some meetings and had opportunity to hear speeches of Ante Beljo, who had come from the Republic of Croatia; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't really know where he came from, but I do know that I listened to him and that he used to come. Excuse me; this was rather at some ceremonies when HDZs were formed. But as an HDZ representative, I never attended a meeting as an HDZ representative. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tuka, you told us that members of the Croat community in Bosnia, after the war broke out in Croatia, began to organise themselves to defend themselves, if need be, and that they were purchasing -- procuring weapons from somewhere, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it true that these weapons and all the other equipment arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina through the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, it came from that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was that the only open route ensuring traffic and access to your area?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, or perhaps a little later, didn't the Muslim community also become aware of the danger and began to organise its defence?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know how to answer that, how or when they began to organise themselves. But when the war broke out, I could see that they had something organised, at least in our case, in Fojnica; how it was elsewhere, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know that the Muslim community used the same routes through the Republic of Croatia to obtain weapons as the Croat community?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I do not really know where they obtained their weapons and how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war broke out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your area, humanitarian aid also arrived there, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both for the Croat and the Muslim communities in your area; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that that humanitarian relief also arrived through the Republic of Croatia -- that is, using the same routes -- regardless of the community it was meant for?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, when you spoke about the so-called Paket communications -- that is, radio communications by computers -- isn't it true that the BH army had an identical system?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Tuka, that there was a possibility for mutually bursting into -- that is, for the mutual tapping of messages and conversations?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't know. Those who set the system up assured us that it was a reliable link and that nobody could bug it, but I don't really know. Possibly it could be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, you described those events when you were asked to try to organise defence in the Fojnica area and the duties you discharged at the time. Sometime in mid-1992, you were actually the head, the chief of the municipal staff of Fojnica, because at that time the brigades had not been established yet, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't really know what we call that, but whatever the case, brigades did not exist as local units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were units which were local in the territory of the municipality, and they were active in the territory of that municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, at the outset. Later on, our men from Fojnica only went to the positions in the Kiseljak municipality, because that is where the boundary was between the Serbs and Croats. So we held that position, and then we went to Jajce, Paklarevo, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you mention it, Mr. Tuka, that units from your municipality went to Paklarevo and other areas, on one occasion when you were visiting them, did you also see HVO units from Novi Travnik and Vitez areas there?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. I can't really say. There were various units there. I don't know. I only visited my units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, how long was this segment of the front line held by your units in Paklarevo?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, but as the head of the municipal staff, sometime in mid-1992, did you have an opportunity to meet Mr. Marijan Skopljak, who was the head of the municipal staff in Vitez at the time?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you exchange experience with him, talk about various things with him, have some agreements or something?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, when you communicated with your colleague in Vitez, did you ever see Mr. Mario Cerkez there?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing that gentleman anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, you mentioned, even though you tried to maintain peace in your area, that there were nevertheless some incidents, and that those incidents were mostly caused by some groups which operated on their own and who set up their own checkpoints at which they, in point of fact, pillaged, robbed people and convoys which passed that way?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, we were in a place where there wasn't much traffic, really, in our territory, so there were not any important checkpoints there. But incidents did happen. Those who called themselves HOS, they caused a lot of trouble. They plundered, looted around, and then of course the tension would go up, and one has to come in town, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you commanded those units, those paramilitary HOS units?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I really don't know who it was. I don't think that those who were in my area were under anyone's command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you try to do something to overcome that tense situation due to the HOS units there?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I once went to Blaz Kraljevic to talk it over with him. I thought he was their commander. But he told me he had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, do you know that about 30 per cent of HOS units were Muslims in your area?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: There were some. Perhaps a couple of them. I wouldn't know the percentage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, you mentioned that Mr. Perica -- and that was the man who had emigrated to the United States, and when the war broke out in Croatia, he came back and joined the Croatian army units in Croatia, and when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he came back to his native land and joined the HVO; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, was it an isolated case, or were there more such people who, from the Republic of Croatia, having fought the JNA and Serb units there, came back to their native land to fight and prepare for defence?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: There were more of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it anything out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, in December 1992, you said you were ordered to set up a brigade; is that so?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I will ask you now something directly regarding the military police. Is it true that those municipalities which did not have brigades of their own did not have military police either; that is, they did not have any military -- municipal military police?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I wouldn't really be able to answer you, to answer accurately that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned those orders you were issued relative to the attack on the village of Dusina, and I should like to ask you to explain to me whether "attack the village of Dusina" means disarm the defenders of that village, the soldiers of that village. Would that be the definition of "attack the village"? Is that what it really means?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Well, that would be the goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it also the duty of military commanders in such a situation -- you told us that the civilian and military population were all mixed together -- to protect the civilian population and to take them out of the area of combat? Is that the duty of military commanders?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't know. It is a very difficult question. It really depends on the situation. It really depends on a given moment, on the situation at a given moment. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, you gave a statement on the 20th of December, 1993, to the Department of the State Security Service in Vitez, but you gave the statement in Fojnica itself. You gave the statement while you were in detention, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you gave that statement under abnormal conditions. Could you describe in a few words what you meant by that phrase?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I had experience from the past that told me that I shouldn't tell the whole truth because I was in such a position. I asked them why that was necessary. They didn't explain. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Tuka, that the statement that you made doesn't really represent a reflection of your free will?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this statement that you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal, as opposed to this one, does that reflect your free will?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: Yes, it does, though there may be some minor errors that could have occurred; but on the whole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Cerkez has no further questions, but we would like to tender into evidence a statement authenticated by this witness, a statement made to the investigators, because we consider it to be very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Mikulicic? Why do you want to exhibit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Because the witness said that this statement is a reflection of his free will, that he verified it on each page with his signature, and in this statement, he discusses in much greater detail the subject matter than it was possible to do in the course of today's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will admit it, for what it's worth. The important thing is the evidence which the witness gives here. Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just pursue for one minute what the nature of the concerns are in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's get on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, just a few points, please. I would ask the usher to kindly hand to the witness Exhibit Z1476 -- sorry; it's not been distributed. I beg your pardon. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could the registry tell us the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D42/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would deal with this matter as quickly as possible, having gone to the time. What is it that you want to raise, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm opposed to these documents being admitted, first of all because they are new and the Defence had no opportunity to ask the witness about them; secondly, these are documents that this witness certainly knows nothing about, because they refer to Mr. Kordic, as I can see from page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have yet to see the document that's being referred to. What is the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was squarely raised, the issue of whether or not a legitimate military position was occupied or held by Mr. Kordic. This was raised on cross, and I would like to have an opportunity, if I may, to pursue it through this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let me see the document that's objected to. Where is the document? I have it. Why was this not produced, if it's relevant, during the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue of challenge to rank was not raised. It has been raised many times and it was simply contested so strongly during cross that I think it appropriate the Court have an opportunity to have a glance at this document now. It would not have come up in our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is going to produce the document? When is it going to be produced?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue in response is simply whether or not there are any references to "honorary" on any titles attributed to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can call evidence. You can produce this in the normal way, but Mr. Naumovski has a point, that you suddenly produce a document which he has no chance of cross-examining on. Now, you can produce this through a witness in the normal way. It's not for this witness, who says he doesn't know anything about it. Yes. Well, we'll return to those documents. Now, have you got anything else you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a brief question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, after you were removed from your position in Fojnica, what was the fate of Mrs. Bosjnak?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: She too resigned to her position in the HDZ -- that is, as president of the HDZ -- and as far as I know, representatives for the municipality were appointed and a new president of the HDZ of Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question. Were you aware of any reprimands that were given by the main staff of the HDZ/BiH to your municipality for any of the so-called illegal activities conducted on behalf of your municipality that were referred to during cross-examination? Was there any complaint at all lodged?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Did you receive any criticism from anyone in the HDZ/BiH in Sarajevo about carrying on the various organisational activities, which were discussed during cross-examination, on behalf of the Fojnica, either HVO or HDZ?

utterances.speaker: Stjepan Tuka
utterances.text: I don't remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tuka, that concludes your examination here. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you all too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there are some matters I want to rise in private session briefly, unless there is any matters you want to deal with in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I was only going to deal with timetable matters. They can be dealt with in private just as easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
